report.source_text: The fungal susceptibility test was reported as an inconclusive result on D + 21 since there is no minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) breakpoint value for Talaromyces from the European Committee on Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing (EUCAST) [4]. Using Aspergillus spp. as a reference, the organism was considered resistance to all common use of antifungal medications (amphotericin B > 8 µg/mL, fluconazole 8 µg/mL, itraconazole > 8 µg/mL, caspofungin > 16 µg/mL) besides voriconazole < 0.5 µg/ml.

report.source_text: In microbiological exams of the PD effluent (PDE) and catheter, the colonies on Sabouraud dextrose agar (SDA) were initially white. However, after 14 days, they gradually developed a membranous aspect with floccose texture and started to darken, turning white to orange and brown (Fig. 1D). Microscopic examination of the colonies demonstrated classic features of the Penicillium genus, including conidiophores and conidia (Fig. 1E-H). The pathogen harvested from the colonies was confirmed the species of T. flavus by molecular phylogeny using ribosomal DNA (ITS and 28 s rDNA) sequences.

clinician.final_diagnosis: Talaromyces flavus peritonitis in a peritoneal dialysis patient (first reported human case)
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 77-year-old Thai female farmer on continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD) since March 2013 presented on 17 June 2019 (day 0) with acute abdominal pain and catheter malfunction. Initial clinical assessment revealed PD effluent with 230/mm³ cells (mixed differential: 35% neutrophils, 35% eosinophils, 30% mononuclear cells) and bedside wet smear microscopy showing filamentous hyaline and septate hyphae, prompting diagnosis of fungal peritonitis. Fungal culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar showed white colonies that developed membranous floccose texture with white-to-orange-to-brown discoloration by day +14. Molecular identification using ribosomal DNA sequencing (ITS and 28S rDNA) confirmed Talaromyces flavus on day +14, representing the first documented human case of this organism. Antifungal susceptibility testing on day +21 demonstrated resistance to amphotericin B (>8 µg/mL), fluconazole (8 µg/mL), itraconazole (>8 µg/mL), and caspofungin (>16 µg/mL), with susceptibility only to voriconazole (MIC <0.5 µg/mL). Treatment was initiated with liposomal amphotericin B 5 mg/kg daily starting day +3 for 14 days, followed by oral itraconazole 400 mg daily starting day +17. By day +21, the patient showed partial clinical response with Edmonton Symptom Assessment System score decreasing from 20 to 7, was afebrile with mild hypertension (140-150/80-90 mmHg), moderate anorexia, and constipation, and was discharged from hospital. However, the patient died at home on day +23 (2 days after discharge) from unknown etiology, attributed to PD-related peritonitis. Environmental investigation identified Talaromyces flavus in the homemade biocontrol agent to which the patient had been exposed on day -17, establishing the likely source of infection.
